sysd-q-090.title: Nearest neighbor search
sysd-q-090.text: In high-dimensional space, checking every point one by one can on average beat the clever indexes. Nearest neighbor search is the optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a query point. Closeness is a dissimilarity function, most often a distance metric such as Euclidean or Manhattan distance over a d-dimensional vector space. A k-nearest neighbor search returns the k closest points instead of one. The simplest exact solution is linear search: compute the distance from the query to every point, in O(dN) time, with no structure to maintain. Space partitioning avoids the full scan. A k-d tree repeatedly bisects the search space, and queries walk from root to leaf in average O(log N) time for randomly distributed points. When tree indexes stop helping in high dimensions, approximate search may return a point within c times the distance to the true nearest. That trades guaranteed answers for speed or memory. Proximity graph methods such as HNSW are the current state of the art for it.

sysd-q-017.title: Proximity service
sysd-q-017.text: Storing each place's latitude and longitude and computing the distance to every place makes a nearby search very inefficient. A proximity service returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants. Its design has two key services. A business service adds, deletes and updates place information and lets customers view details. A location-based service returns the places near a given location and radius. The geohash algorithm speeds up the search. It divides the planet into four quadrants along the prime meridian and equator, then keeps dividing each grid into four. A grid is named by alternating longitude and latitude bits. Nearby places in a grid are then found with a prefix match on the geohash column, for example geohash LIKE '01%'. Geohash has limits: one grid can hold very many places, such as downtown New York, and another none, such as the ocean. More complicated algorithms optimize the process.

sysd-q-089.title: Dynamic pricing
sysd-q-089.text: Uber has capped how high surge pricing can go in emergencies since 2015. Dynamic pricing, also called surge pricing, sets flexible prices from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand. That encourages buying when demand is low and discourages it when demand is high. In some sectors economists see it as a more efficient allocation of limited resources. Algorithmic pricing does this automatically, to maximize the seller's profit. It is often criticized as price gouging, so operators add guardrails. Drivers, meanwhile, may hold off accepting rides until surge raises fares.

sysd-q-016.title: Designing a ride-hailing service like Uber
sysd-q-016.text:
A ride-hailing service like Uber lets customers see nearby cabs with ETA and pricing, book a cab and see the driver's location. Drivers accept or deny rides, see the pickup location and mark the trip complete on reaching the destination. The system needs high availability with minimal latency, and it must scale. Trip ratings, payment processing, and metrics and analytics are extended requirements. Assume 100 million daily active users, 1 million drivers and 10 million rides daily, with 10 actions per user. That is 1 billion requests daily, or 12K requests per second. At 400 bytes per message, storage is about 400 GB a day and about 1.4 PB over 10 years. Minimum ingress bandwidth is around 5 MB per second.

The tables hold customers, drivers, trips (source, destination, status), cabs (registration number, type), and ratings and payments by trip ID. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Request a ride takes a customer ID, source and destination. Cancel takes a customer ID and an optional reason. Accept or deny takes a driver ID and ride ID, start or end uses a driver ID and trip ID, and rating takes a score. The services are microservices that own their data: customer, driver, ride (ride matching and quadtree aggregation), trip, payment, notification and analytics. They communicate over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

A customer requests a ride with source, destination, cab type and payment method. The ride service finds nearby drivers and the ETA and broadcasts the request. Once a driver accepts, the customer sees the driver's live location and ETA. Pulling location by periodic HTTP requests or long polling does not scale: it adds request overhead, and most responses are empty. A WebSocket push model delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike unidirectional Server-Sent Events.

Finding nearby drivers is the hard query, the one {{ref:sysd-q-017}} describes. A radius query on PostgreSQL or MySQL is too slow at scale. Geohash encodes coordinates as hierarchical base-32 strings, so the customer's geohash is compared with drivers' geohashes, indexed in memory. A quadtree, whose internal nodes have four children, splits two-dimensional space to search points in a range efficiently. Split a node only past a threshold, update it on each driver location update, and cache the latest updates in Redis.

Race conditions arise when many customers request rides at once, so the ride matching logic is wrapped in a mutex and every action is transactional. Nearby drivers are ranked by parameters such as average rating, relevance and past feedback, so the best are notified first. Under high demand, surge pricing temporarily raises prices in reaction to increased demand and limited supply, as {{ref:sysd-q-089}} describes. Payments go to a third-party processor such as Stripe or PayPal, with a webhook capturing payment data. Push notifications flow through a message queue or broker such as Kafka to {{ref:sysd-q-074}} or {{ref:sysd-q-075}}.

Shard by region, such as zip codes, with consistent hashing against uneven load. Cache recent customer and driver locations in Redis or Memcached with LRU eviction, refilling from the database on a miss. Remove single points of failure with multiple service instances, load balancers between clients, servers, databases and caches, read replicas and replicated caches. A dedicated broker such as Kafka or NATS makes notifications robust. The thing to remember: the heart of the design is the nearby-driver lookup, and the rest is keeping it fast and safe when many riders ask at once.

sysd-q-018.title: Uber's technology stack
sysd-q-018.text:
Uber built its own React framework, Fusion.js, for its web frontend. It also uses visualization.js for geospatial visualization. The mobile apps use the RIB architecture with VIPER instead of MVC, in Swift for iOS and Java for Android. Uber Gateway is a dynamic configuration on top of NGINX. Client-server communication uses {{ref:sysd-msg-005}} and QUIC, and APIs are defined with Apache Thrift.

Backend services use Spring Boot for Java, uAct for event-driven architecture and Cadence for asynchronous workflow orchestration. Flipr, later UCDP, is a unified configuration store, and H3 is a location-index store library. The main OLTP store, the database for live transactions, is the strongly consistent DocStore, which employs MySQL and PostgreSQL with the RocksDB engine. Big data uses the Hadoop family with Hudi and Parquet file formats and Alluxio as cache. Time-series data is in Pinot and AresDB. Hive, Spark and Marmaray process data, and {{ref:sysd-msg-036}} and Flink handle messaging and streaming. DevOps uses a monorepo with devpod environments and Spinnaker for continuous delivery, with uMetric for metrics, uMonitor for alarms and M3 as the observability database.

sysd-q-049.title: Web crawler
sysd-q-049.text: One photo gallery can look like 48 different pages to a crawler. With four sort orders, three thumbnail sizes, two file formats and an option to hide user content, it serves the same content under 48 different URLs. A web crawler is an Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads. It starts from a list of seed URLs and fetches those pages. It finds their hyperlinks and adds them to the list of URLs still to visit, called the crawl frontier. Frontier URLs are visited recursively under policies for selection ({{ref:sysd-q-050}}), re-visit ({{ref:sysd-q-053}}), politeness ({{ref:sysd-q-054}}) and parallelization. The web is so large that a crawler can download only a limited number of pages in a given time, so it must prioritize. A parallel crawler runs multiple processes, so it needs a policy for assigning newly found URLs: two processes can discover the same URL and download the page twice. Crawlers typically identify themselves in the User-agent field of the HTTP request.

sysd-q-055.title: Robots exclusion protocol
sysd-q-055.text: A polite crawler checks before it fetches. The robots exclusion protocol, usually called robots.txt, is the standard by which a website tells visiting web crawlers which portions of the site they may visit. A site owner puts a robots.txt file at the root of the site. A compliant robot fetches it before any other file, uses it to decide which links to follow, and assumes no limits if the file is missing. The protocol is purely advisory and relies on voluntary compliance. Malicious bots may ignore it or use it to find disallowed paths. Developed in 1994, it was published as a proposed standard, RFC 9309, in September 2022. The standard sets no visit interval, though that is the most effective way to avoid overload. The non-standard Crawl-delay is read differently: Yandex takes seconds between visits, Bing a window of 1 to 30 seconds, and Google ignores it. Robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers act at finer grain, but only after the page loads, whereas robots.txt acts before the request.

sysd-q-054.title: Crawl politeness policy
sysd-q-054.text: The first proposed delay between requests to one site was 60 seconds. At that rate a site of more than 100,000 pages would take over 2 months to download. A crawl politeness policy is the set of rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits. Crawlers fetch data faster and deeper than human searchers, so one making many requests per second or downloading large files can cripple a site's performance. The costs include network bandwidth, server overload and poorly written crawlers that can crash servers or routers. The robots exclusion protocol only partly solves this. It says which parts of a server to avoid but suggests no interval between visits, the most effective way to avoid overload. Major search engines support an extra Crawl-delay parameter in robots.txt giving the seconds to wait between requests. Cho uses 10 seconds, WIRE 15 seconds and Dill et al. 1 second. The Mercator crawler is adaptive: if a download from a server took t seconds, it waits 10t seconds before fetching the next page from it.

sysd-q-053.title: Crawl re-visit policy
sysd-q-053.text: A crawl of part of the web can take weeks or months, and the web does not wait. Creations, updates and deletions happen meanwhile, and the search engine pays a cost for holding an outdated copy. The crawl re-visit policy is the rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale. The usual cost functions are freshness, a binary measure of whether the local copy is accurate, and age, a measure of how outdated the copy is. A uniform policy re-visits all pages at the same frequency. A proportional policy re-visits pages that change more often more frequently, in proportion to their estimated change rate. The surprise is that uniform beats proportional on average freshness, because a proportional policy spends crawls on rapidly changing pages whose freshness lasts only briefly. The optimal policy is closer to uniform. To keep average freshness high, ignore pages that change too often. To keep average age low, raise access frequency sub-linearly with a page's rate of change.

sysd-q-050.title: Crawl selection policy
sysd-q-050.text: Even large search engines cover only part of the public web: a 2009 study showed they index no more than 40-70% of the indexable web. A crawl selection policy decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking them by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched. The downloaded fraction should hold the most relevant pages, not a random sample. So the policy needs an importance metric built from a page's intrinsic quality, its popularity in links or visits, and sometimes its URL. It must work with partial information, since the full set of pages is unknown while crawling. A breadth-first crawl captures pages with high {{ref:sysd-q-109}} early, because the most important pages have many links from numerous hosts. OPIC gives each page an initial sum of cash, split equally among the pages it links to. The crawler downloads the frontier pages holding the most cash first. Some crawlers skip any URL containing a "?" to avoid endless URL traps (see {{ref:sysd-q-113}}), though this is unreliable when a site rewrites URLs.

sysd-q-056.title: How search engines work
sysd-q-056.text: When you search, you are not searching the web. You are searching an index the engine built earlier. Search engines work through three processes: crawling pages, indexing what was collected, and serving ranked results for queries. Crawlers start from a list of known pages, the seeds, and follow links to discover and download new pages. The collected information is analyzed and organized into a massive index. The engine extracts keywords, content type, freshness, language and other signals to learn what each page is about and how relevant it may be to queries. To serve a query, the engine first analyzes it for meaning and intent, identifying keywords, recognizing synonyms and interpreting context. It then retrieves pages from the index by matching the query's keywords with indexed content, and ranks the retrieved pages by relevance and other factors.

sysd-q-108.title: Search engine indexing
sysd-q-108.text: Without an index, an engine would scan every document in the corpus. An index of 10,000 documents can be queried within milliseconds, while a sequential scan of 10,000 large documents could take hours. Search engine indexing is the collecting, parsing and storing of data so that information can be retrieved quickly and accurately. The index is paid for with extra storage and a considerably longer update time. Parsing breaks documents into tokens for the forward and inverted indices. With several languages, identifying each document's language comes first, because later steps such as stemming depend on it. Tokenizing is hard when words are not delineated by whitespace, as in Chinese or Japanese, so a parser is often built per language. Indexing is a producer-consumer chain: the crawler fills the corpus, the forward index consumes it, and the inverted index consumes the forward index. That lets indexers work asynchronously. Adding a document while the index keeps answering queries invites race conditions. A simple uncompressed index for 2 billion web pages would hold 500 billion word entries, about 2500 gigabytes at 5 bytes per word. Compression shrinks it at the cost of compression and decompression time.

sysd-q-109.title: PageRank
sysd-q-109.text: PageRank treats every link as a vote. It is a link analysis algorithm, used by Google Search, that gives each page in a hyperlinked set a numerical weight measuring its relative importance. A page linked from many high-PageRank pages gets a high rank itself, so the rank is defined recursively. The web is a graph, with pages as nodes and hyperlinks as edges. The output is a probability distribution: the chance that a person randomly clicking links lands on each page. Each page passes its PageRank equally to the pages it links to. The damping factor d, generally around 0.85, is the chance the surfer keeps following links; otherwise they jump to a random page. The values are computed iteratively until they stop changing, and the original paper reports 322 million links converging in 52 iterations. It favors older pages, since a new page has few links, and paid links and link farms can manipulate it.

sysd-q-111.title: Cosine similarity
sysd-q-111.text: Two documents of different lengths can still be about the same thing. Cosine similarity captures that. It is the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors, their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. It depends only on the angle, not the magnitudes, and lies in [-1, +1]: proportional vectors score +1, orthogonal ones 0, opposite ones -1. In text mining each word is a coordinate and a document is the vector of its word counts. The measure then shows how alike two documents are in subject matter, regardless of length. Its cost is low for sparse vectors, because only the non-zero coordinates count.

sysd-q-112.title: Sitemaps
sysd-q-112.text: A sitemap tells a crawler what to visit, where robots.txt tells it what to avoid. It is an XML protocol that lets a webmaster tell search engines which URLs on a site are available for crawling. That makes it a URL inclusion protocol, complementing robots.txt, a URL exclusion protocol. It guarantees neither indexing nor ranking, but it helps crawlers find isolated URLs. The file has a required loc for each URL and optional lastmod, changefreq and priority (0.0 to 1.0, default 0.5), which are only hints. One sitemap holds at most 50,000 URLs or 50MiB uncompressed, and a sitemap index file may list up to 50,000 sitemaps.

sysd-q-057.title: Deep web crawling
sysd-q-057.text: A vast number of pages sit in the deep or invisible web, where regular crawlers cannot find them. Deep web crawling is the effort to reach them. They are usually reachable only by submitting queries to a database, and no links point to them. Google's Sitemaps protocol and mod oai are intended to let such resources be discovered, though it also multiplies the number of links to crawl. Screen scraping software can be customized to query a web form repeatedly and aggregate the results. Pages built on AJAX cause problems for crawlers, and Google has proposed a format of AJAX calls its bot can recognize and index.

sysd-q-052.title: Focused crawler
sysd-q-052.text: A crawler does not have to want every page. A focused crawler, also called a topical crawler, tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic. A page's importance can be expressed as its similarity to a query. The main problem is predicting a page's text similarity to the query before downloading it. One predictor is the anchor text of links, and another is the full content of pages already visited. Performance depends mostly on how rich in links the topic is, and a focused crawl usually relies on a general web search engine to supply starting points.

sysd-q-051.title: URL normalization
sysd-q-051.text: To a crawler, two different strings can name one page. URL normalization, also called URL canonicalization, modifies and standardizes a URL in a consistent way, so that one resource has one form. Crawlers usually normalize URLs to avoid crawling the same resource more than once. Typical normalizations convert URLs to lowercase, remove "." and ".." segments, and add trailing slashes to a non-empty path component.

sysd-q-113.title: Spider trap
sysd-q-113.text: A calendar whose pages keep linking to the next day, and the next, never ends. That is a spider trap: a set of web pages that makes a crawler issue an infinite number of requests or crash. Some traps are made on purpose, to catch spambots or crawlers that waste bandwidth; others are accidents. Typical forms are indefinitely deep directory structures, dynamic pages that produce an unbounded number of documents, and session ids that require cookies. A trap acts like an infinite loop and can crash a poorly written crawler. Sites with traps usually list them in robots.txt, so a polite bot that obeys it stays out.

sysd-q-110.title: Jaccard index
sysd-q-110.text: How alike are two sets? The Jaccard index answers with one number: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union. It is a normalized measure of overlap, from 0 for sets with nothing in common to 1 for equal sets. The Jaccard distance is 1 minus it. Unlike the simple matching coefficient, it ignores attributes absent from both sets, so it suits sparse data. For documents, the resemblance of two documents is the Jaccard coefficient of their shingle sets, as {{ref:sysd-q-114}} describes. MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing approximate it at scale from compact fixed-size signatures.

sysd-q-114.title: W-shingling
sysd-q-114.text: The phrase "a rose is a rose is a rose" has five runs of four words, but only three of them are different. A w-shingling is a set of unique shingles, each a run of w contiguous tokens (n-grams) from a document, used to measure how similar two documents are. Repeats collapse in the set, which is why the example gives three. The resemblance of two documents is the size of the intersection of their shinglings divided by the size of the union, from 0 to 1. That is the {{ref:sysd-q-110}}.

sysd-q-048.title: Designing a web crawler
sysd-q-048.text:
A web crawler feeds a search engine. The service must crawl a list of URLs, build a reverse index of words to pages and generate static titles and snippets. A user enters a search term and sees matching pages with those titles and snippets. It must be highly available and produce search results fast. The crawler must not get stuck in an infinite loop, which happens if the link graph contains a cycle. Search analytics and personalized results are out of scope, and only anonymous users are supported. Search traffic is not evenly distributed: some searches are very popular, while others are executed only once.

The assumptions are 1 billion links to crawl and a refresh rate of about once per week, more often for popular sites. They also include 4 billion links crawled each month, 500 KB average stored size per page and 100 billion searches per month. That makes 2 PB of stored page content per month, which is 500 KB per page times 4 billion links, and 72 PB in 3 years. The load is 1,600 write requests per second and 40,000 search requests per second.

The data model is two tables. links_to_crawl is ranked initially by overall site popularity, and crawled_links stores processed links with their page signatures. Both could live in a key-value NoSQL database, with Redis sorted sets keeping the link ranking. If the initial list is not reasonable, the crawler can be seeded with popular sites that link to outside content, such as Yahoo or DMOZ.

The Crawler Service runs in a loop. It takes the top ranked link and checks crawled_links for a similar page signature. If a similar page exists, it lowers the link's priority, which prevents a cycle. Otherwise it crawls the link and queues a job for the Reverse Index Service and one for the Document Service, which makes the static title and snippet. It generates the page signature, removes the link from links_to_crawl and inserts the link and signature into crawled_links.

Duplicate URLs can be removed with sort and unique for small lists. With 1 billion links to crawl, MapReduce can output only the entries that have a frequency of 1. Detecting duplicate content is more complex. Generate a signature from each page's contents and compare signatures for similarity, using an algorithm such as the {{ref:sysd-q-110}} or {{ref:sysd-q-111}}. Each crawl result carries a timestamp of the last crawl. After a default period, say one week, all pages are refreshed, and frequently updated or popular sites are refreshed sooner. A robots.txt file could give webmasters control of crawl frequency, as {{ref:sysd-q-054}} explains.

A search goes from the client to a reverse-proxy web server, then to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations. It asks the Reverse Index Service for matching documents, ranks them and returns the top ones, and the Document Service returns titles and snippets. The public API is REST, and internal calls could use RPC.

Popular queries can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached. That cuts response times, protects the Reverse Index Service and Document Service, and absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. Those two services will likely need heavy sharding and federation. The crawler itself can keep its own periodically refreshed DNS lookup and pool many open connections, and it needs enough bandwidth, since crawling is bandwidth intensive. The thing to remember: the crawler must never fetch what it has already seen, and the page signature check is what breaks the cycle.

openers.design-a-ride-hailing-service-like-uber: Open a ride-hailing app and the screen shows nearby cabs, an ETA and a price. This chapter takes that screen apart. It starts with nearest neighbor search, the problem of finding the point closest to a query point, and the proximity service that applies it to places within a radius. It adds dynamic pricing, then ends with the worked Uber design and a look at Uber's technology stack.
openers.design-a-web-crawler: A web crawler visits the Web page by page, following links from a list of starting addresses, so that a search engine has something to index. The web is too large to fetch in full, so a crawler needs rules for what to download, when to return and how to avoid overloading the sites it visits. This chapter covers those rules, the robots.txt standard that sites use to set limits, and what happens to the pages afterward: indexing, ranking with PageRank and measuring how similar two pages are. It closes with a worked design for a crawler and the search engine behind it.

reviews.design-a-ride-hailing-service-like-uber: Two ideas carry this chapter's design: find the nearest cabs quickly, and price the ride by demand. Nearest neighbor search names the problem, a proximity service solves it for places within a radius, and geohash and quadtree are the structures that avoid measuring the distance to every driver. Dynamic pricing answers peaks in demand, with guardrails such as Uber's cap in emergencies since 2015. The worked design adds WebSockets for live location, a mutex around ride matching and sharding by region, and Uber's own stack shows the tools behind it, from gRPC and QUIC to DocStore and Kafka.
reviews.design-a-web-crawler: A crawler is a set of rules wrapped around a loop. Selection decides what to download, re-visit decides when to come back, and politeness and robots.txt decide how fast, while sitemaps, deep web crawling and focused crawlers widen or narrow what it can reach, and spider traps and duplicate URLs waste its effort. What it collects becomes an index that PageRank helps rank, and cosine similarity, the Jaccard index and W-shingling compare the pages inside it. The worked design puts the pieces together: a ranked list of links, a page signature to stop cycles, and a reverse index to answer 40,000 search requests per second.
